item.title: Indonesia’s most dangerous fires are burning underground
item.description:
Waypoint is curating and commenting on third-party reporting. Original publisher: ScienceDaily.
Summary: Indonesia’s dangerous peat fires are surging early in the 2026 fire season as a strengthening El Niño and severe drought dry out wetlands that can burn underground for months. These slow smoldering fires are especially destructive because they release far more fine particles and several pollutants than typical tropical forest fires, while thick smoke can make them difficult for satellites to detect.

item.title: The local costs of remote sensing: Examining the ethics of laser scanning in tropical forests
item.description:
Waypoint is curating and commenting on third-party reporting. Original publisher: Phys.org.
Summary: Laser scanning, often referred to as lidar, has rapidly transformed how tropical forest regions are studied, monitored and understood across academic disciplines. The technology enables researchers to peer through dense forest canopies, rapidly providing high-resolution scans of the landscape below. This growing observational power is central to the scientific value of remote sensing technologies but also brings into focus the conditions, interests and power structures under which they are used.

item.title: Back-to-back Arctic storms can double sea ice loss
item.description:
Waypoint is curating and commenting on third-party reporting. Original publisher: ScienceDaily.
Summary: Scientists have found that Arctic cyclones become especially destructive when several strike one after another. These storm clusters cause about twice as much sea ice loss as isolated cyclones, with impacts that persist roughly two and a half times longer. As Arctic ice becomes thinner and weaker, the damage from these storms appears to be increasing, potentially creating a feedback loop that accelerates future ice loss.
